title: Who Knew We Were in Violent Agreement?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article examines 'violent agreement,' the phenomenon of two parties arguing forcefully for positions they actually share because neither is truly listening. It suggests that occasional violent agreement is a normal lapse, but that leaders who fall into it repeatedly and with multiple people are revealing something deeper than stubbornness. The piece links a chronic need to be right to underlying insecurity, arguing that such leaders use 'being right' as a way to manage self-doubt rather than as a genuine pursuit of truth. It offers a light intervention: naming the pattern out loud, and asking the leader why they argue so hard when others already agree, as a way to build self-awareness. The archivist notes this piece pairs naturally with other Admired Leadership essays on ego, insecurity, and listening.
points: 'Violent agreement' occurs when two people argue past each other despite actually sharing the same view.
Occasional violent agreement is normal, but a repeated pattern across many people signals a deeper issue.
A chronic need to be right often masks underlying insecurity rather than reflecting confidence.
Being right can function like a narcotic that eases a leader's self-doubt at the expense of relationships.
Gently naming the pattern and asking why the leader argues so hard when others agree can build self-awareness.
quotes: The extreme need to be right prevents people from listening to what others are saying — even when they are in agreement.
Parties who argue strongly against each other when they actually view the issue in the same way are said to be in violent agreement.
It speaks to a much deeper insecurity that will eventually undermine the leader’s ability to succeed with others.
Being right becomes a narcotic, easing the self-doubt and uncertainty they won’t admit to.
The more they insist on being right or more right, the more their credibility tumbles in the eyes of those who witness it.
Convincing someone who needs to be right that they are sometimes wrong is never fun. But it is the essential work of those who care.
